finding.claim: Every authorization decision trusts g.user, which notes.py never sets. If the unseen middleware derives identity from client-controlled input, all checks are bypassed. Severity depends on code not in this directory.
finding.sink: require_view (line 28), can_edit (line 35), require_edit (line 44), ownership/shared checks in notes.py:7-22

trace.note: can_view compares owner and shared against g.user
write endpoint PUT consumes g.user via can_edit
share endpoint POST consumes g.user via require_edit

finding.guards_checked: Ownership and sharing checks on read, write and share. Nothing in notes.py establishes identity. As written, requests fail with AttributeError, so this cannot be tested from this directory.

verdict.guard_found: Ownership/sharing checks: can_view (notes.py:7-8) gates require_view (notes.py:11-13, abort(403)) on read at line 28; can_edit (notes.py:16-17) gates require_edit (notes.py:20-22) on share at line 44 and an inline `if not can_edit` with abort(403) on write at lines 35-36. All use return values that are tested and abort on failure. No code in notes.py assigns g.user, so no control establishes identity.
verdict.reason: The per-note checks at notes.py:8, 17, 12-13 and 21-22 are correctly enforced, but g.user is never assigned in notes.py, so whether any caller can impersonate a user depends on middleware not in this directory; as written every request raises AttributeError at notes.py:28, 35 and 44 (fail-closed), so the claim cannot be confirmed or refuted here.

finding.claim: The share list accepts values that are not principals. An owner can share with null, so an anonymous identity matching None can read the note, if the unseen middleware maps anonymous requests to None.
finding.source: request.json['user'] at line 45, reachable only by the owner (require_edit at line 44)
finding.sink: can_view membership check at line 8, reached via read at line 29

trace.note: shared.append(request.json['user']) with no type or existence validation; null appends None
jsonify(n) returns note body to anonymous caller

finding.guards_checked: require_edit limits who can share. No validation of type, format or existence of the shared user. Same risk applies to empty string or any sentinel the auth layer uses for anonymous. Requires unseen middleware to map anonymous to None or a matching value.

verdict.guard_found: require_edit (notes.py:20-22, called at line 44) restricts the share endpoint to the note owner. can_view (notes.py:7-8) and require_view (notes.py:11-13) gate the read path, but they are not an effective block here since the premise is that the shared value matches the caller.
verdict.reason: The trace is accurate (notes.py:44-45 and 26-29 match the description), but the only actor who can append to the share list is the owner (notes.py:44 via require_edit), who already controls who sees their note, and the anonymous-maps-to-None premise depends on middleware that is not in the codebase, so the claimed exposure is unverified and not an attacker-reachable escalation.

finding.claim: Note existence can be probed. Missing IDs raise KeyError and return HTTP 500, while existing IDs without access return 403, so an attacker can tell which IDs exist.

trace.note: NOTES[nid] raises KeyError for unknown id, yielding 500
abort(403) for existing note without view access
abort(403) for existing note without edit access

finding.guards_checked: 403 responses are correct for unauthorized access. No 404 handling exists. Impact depends on how guessable note IDs are.

verdict.guard_found: None blocks the probe. There is no KeyError handler or 404 conversion in notes.py; the only checks are require_view/require_edit at notes.py:12-13 and :20-22, which abort(403) only after the lookup has already succeeded. Lookups at notes.py:27, :34 and :43 raise KeyError first and return 500. The g.user setter (auth middleware) is not in this directory, so the attacker is assumed to be an authenticated user with a g.user value.
verdict.reason: NOTES[nid] at notes.py:27 raises KeyError for unknown IDs (500), while an existing note fails require_view at notes.py:28 with abort(403) (lines 12-13), and no 404 handling exists in the file, so an authenticated user can tell which note IDs exist. Impact is limited to existence disclosure and depends on how guessable the IDs are, and g.user's setter is outside the reviewed code.

finding.claim: Owner-driven resource growth and missing revocation. shared.append has no deduplication or size limit, body at line 37 has no size limit, and MAX_CONTENT_LENGTH is not set in this file. No endpoint removes a shared user or deletes a note, so read access is permanent.
finding.sink: shared list growth and NOTES body storage in memory

trace.note: no MAX_CONTENT_LENGTH configured in this file

finding.guards_checked: Only the owner can trigger either path (require_edit at line 44, can_edit at line 35). No revocation or deletion endpoint exists in this file.

verdict.guard_found: require_edit (notes.py:20-22, called at line 44) aborts with 403 unless note["owner"] == user; can_edit (notes.py:16-17, checked at line 35) gates the PUT body write. Both are real checks whose failures abort before the effect. No size limit or MAX_CONTENT_LENGTH is set in this file.
verdict.reason: Both sinks (notes.py:45 append and notes.py:37 body assignment) are reachable only by the note owner (require_edit at notes.py:44, can_edit at notes.py:35), who already has full write and share power over that note, so the growth is self-inflicted and not a privilege boundary crossing. The missing revocation and size limit are real hardening gaps but do not let an attacker gain access or exceed their role, so this is not a vulnerability as claimed.
